endorsements.quote: Initial “silent mode” deployment, in which models run in the background without influencing care, allows prospective validation against local outcomes and the assessment of calibration within a specific institution.
For this reason, AI outputs should be regarded as advisory rather than determinative, with final decisions remaining under clinician oversight.
Embedding these tools within electronic health record systems is likely to be essential for usability.

Prospective studies should move beyond discrimination metrics alone and assess whether AI-supported care improves clinically meaningful outcomes, such as complications, length of stay, resource utilization, or shared decision-making quality.
External validation across diverse centers and healthcare systems remains necessary to establish generalizability and detect performance drift over time [ 5 ] .
Standardized reporting frameworks and transparent model development practices are also required to strengthen reproducibility and facilitate comparison across studies [ 3 ] .

unlisted_practices: Use AI risk prediction as a complement to established risk scores (hybrid framework) rather than replacing validated conventional models.
Design decision-support interfaces to display key drivers of risk and avoid excessive alerts that contribute to cognitive overload.
Conduct human-factors research on clinician trust, interface design, and workflow integration.
Perform ongoing performance surveillance after deployment.

screen.reason: This is an editorial commenting on the implementation barriers and best practices for deploying AI risk stratification models in cardiothoracic surgery.
